title: Coding-Agent Evals in Parallel GPU Sandboxes: What to Know (2026)
summary: How coding-agent evals like SWE-bench run in parallel GPU sandboxes: HumanEval vs SWE-bench, when evals need a GPU, preemption and cost per run.
body_markdown:
Coding-agent evals run benchmark tasks in isolated sandboxes. They do so in parallel to cut a full run from days to hours. These coding-agents edit real repositories and execute commands, making isolation a security requirement.


Many eval guides assume the model sits behind an API. But in some cases, the model being tested or used to judge results needs a GPU within the sandbox. This changes implementation and costs to address parallelism, preemption and required resources.


**Takeaways**


- **Each eval task runs in its own sandbox** to contain agent actions and keep results reproducible.
- **Parallelism speeds up the process:** 32 parallel runtimes cut a full SWE-bench Lite run to several hours.
- **Some evals need a GPU in the sandbox** when using self-hosted, fine-tuned or judge models.
- **A 300-task SWE-bench Lite run costs about $160-$265** on H100 sandboxes.


Benchmark figures and provider details in this guide were verified in October 2026.


## A Brief History of Coding-Agent Benchmarks


Coding benchmarks have moved from single functions to whole repositories. Along the way, the infrastructure they need also changed: function-level benchmarks needed little more than a process per problem, while repository-level tasks each need a full sandbox.


### Function-Level Benchmarks: CodeXGLUE, APPS, HumanEval and MBPP


2021 was a big year for code generation benchmarks:


- [CodeXGLUE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04664) came first, in February, with 10 tasks across 14 datasets for code understanding and generation.
- [APPS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09938) followed in May with 10,000 Python problems.
- HumanEval arrived in July, with 164 Python problems, each with a function signature, a docstring and unit tests.[OpenAI introduced it](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374) alongside Codex, together with the pass@k metric: the probability that at least one of k generated samples passes all the tests.
- [MBPP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07732) followed in August with 974 entry-level problems written by crowd workers, each with three test cases.


### Stronger Tests and Fresh Problems: HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench


As models improved, two weaknesses of these benchmarks surfaced: thin tests and solutions in training data.


[EvalPlus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) improved tests in 2023. HumanEval averages about 10 tests per problem, while its HumanEval+ extension averages about 764. Across 26 models, pass@k dropped by 19%-29%, and some model rankings changed.


[LiveCodeBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07974) fixed widely available solutions in 2024. This eval collects new problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder and CodeForces, so scores can be limited to problems published after a model's training data ends. It also tests self-repair and predicting a program's output, not only writing code.


Both still grade one program at a time against tests, so they put little demand on sandbox infrastructure.


### SWE-bench


SWE-bench moved evaluation from functions to repositories. All[2,294 tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) pair a real GitHub issue with tests. The agent reads the codebase, edits files and produces a patch.


Two SWE-bench subsets became common for coding-agent evaluation:


- [SWE-bench Lite](https://www.swebench.com/) has 300 tasks, which makes it cheaper to run.
- [SWE-bench Verified has 500 tasks](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) screened by human annotators for clear issue descriptions and fair tests.


In February 2026,[OpenAI stopped evaluating SWE-bench Verified](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/) , because an audit of 138 problems that o3 didn't consistently solve found that 59.4% had material test or description issues. In addition, every frontier model tested could reproduce the original fix or verbatim problem details for some tasks.


OpenAI recommends[SWE-bench Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16941) instead. This is a separate benchmark with new tasks rather than a subset of SWE-bench, and has 1,865 tasks from 41 repositories. Its held-out and commercial splits aren't public, which makes training-data contamination less likely.


## Why Coding-Agent Evals Run in Sandboxes


Coding-agent evals run in sandboxes for two reasons:


1. Safety: The agent executes untrusted commands which could damage the machine without a sandbox.
2. Reproducibility: Every task starts under the same conditions, and a previous task's installed packages or leftover processes can't change another's result.

## When Evals Need a GPU Inside the Sandbox


Coding-agent evals need a GPU in the sandbox only when a model runs inside the eval environment. When an API serves the model being tested, the sandbox runs only the repository, the shell and the tests. And CPUs can handle that workload.


### Evaluating Self-Hosted or Fine-Tuned Models


Self-hosted and fine-tuned models need a GPU wherever the eval serves them. Placing the model in the same sandbox as the task keeps each eval self-contained. The model, the repository and the tests start together and disappear together, which suits models that fit on a single GPU.


### Judge and Reward Models


Judge and reward models need a GPU when an eval scores output with a model instead of, or alongside, unit tests. A judge model rates code quality, and a reward model scores trajectories. The same reward models appear in[RL environments for agent training](https://www.thundercompute.com/blog/rl-environments-gpu-sandboxes) , so eval and RL infrastructure often look alike.


### Evaluating GPU Code Such as CUDA Kernels


Evals that grade CUDA code have to run that code, so each task sandbox needs a GPU.[KernelBench](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.10517) gives a model 250 PyTorch tasks and asks it to write a faster CUDA kernel for each one. The eval then runs the kernel on the GPU to check that its output matches the PyTorch reference and to time it against that reference.


The kernel can compile on CPU. But timing is only reliable when the kernel has a dedicated GPU to itself.


## Running Evals in Parallel


Parallelism is the main way to speed up coding-agent eval. OpenHands reports that a single SWE-bench Lite task can take about 10 minutes, so sequentially the 300-tasks take around two days to run. Running 32 tasks in parallel cut this down to several hours.


That speedup is why eval tooling is now built around parallelism:


- [CoreWeave's SWE-bench guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sandboxes/client/guides/swebench) runs each instance in its own sandbox, and its configurable worker count sets how many instances run at once.
- [SWE-ReX](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-ReX) (the SWE-agent team's remote execution framework) runs agent sessions across remote sandbox backends in parallel.


### Setting Concurrency and Timeouts


Eval concurrency is capped by capacity, quota and budget, not by the benchmark. Most harnesses expose a worker count. The right worker count is the most sandboxes a team can run without hitting capacity errors or overloading a shared model server.


Per-task timeouts matter as much as concurrency. A timeout stops a stuck agent from holding a sandbox, and its resources, for the rest of the run. Set the timeout slightly above the typical task length, and record timeouts as failures, not silent drops.


## Why Preemption Skews Eval Results


Preemption adds noise to coding-agent eval results. A sandbox reclaimed mid-task must be configured to restart the task adding cost and delay, and untracked failures quietly lower the pass rate.


Several GPU sandbox options can be preempted.[Modal's GPU Sandboxes are subject to preemption](https://modal.com/docs/guide/preemption) , and[Daytona's spot GPU sandboxes can also be terminated without notice](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/sandboxes/#spot-gpu-sandboxes) . Evals on preemptible capacity should log every retry, so a reported score reflects the model rather than the infrastructure.

Thunder Compute's GPU sandboxes provide ephemeral, API-created environments running in their own Firecracker microVM (a lightweight, hardware-isolated VM) with a GPU attached.


Thunder Compute sandboxes are never preempted, so a task that starts finishes, and pass rates carry no hidden retries. H100 sandboxes cost $2.95/hr, $1/hr below Daytona's on-demand H100. A100 80GB sandboxes cost $1.95/hr for smaller models under test, with no region multipliers or egress fees.

## Last Thoughts on Coding-Agent Evals


Coding-agent evals have moved from single-function benchmarks like HumanEval to repository-level tasks like SWE-bench, which introduced the need for sandboxes. One sandbox per task keeps results clean, and parallelism turns a multi-day run into an afternoon.


A GPU belongs in the sandbox only when a model runs there; when it does, pick a layout, cap every task with a timeout and run on capacity that won't reclaim a task halfway through.


## FAQ


### What Is HumanEval?


HumanEval is a benchmark of 164 hand-written Python programming problems with unit tests, introduced by OpenAI in 2021. It scores models with pass@k, the probability that at least one of k generated solutions passes every test.


### What Is SWE-bench Lite?


SWE-bench Lite is a 300-task subset of SWE-bench chosen to be cheaper to run. SWE-bench Verified is a separate 500-task subset that human annotators screened for clear issue descriptions and fair tests.


### Why Run Coding-Agent Evals in Sandboxes?


Sandboxes keep coding agents from damaging the host, because agents execute commands the model chose. A fresh sandbox per task also keeps results independent, since nothing one task changes can affect the next.


### Do Coding-Agent Evals Need a GPU Sandbox?


Coding-agent evals need a GPU Sandbox only when a model runs inside the eval environment, such as a self-hosted or fine-tuned model under test, or a judge or reward model. Evals against an API-served model only need CPU sandboxes.


### How Much Does a Coding-Agent Eval Run Cost?


A 300-task SWE-bench Lite run uses roughly 50 GPU-hours at about 10 minutes per task. On an H100 sandbox, that costs about $194 on Thunder Compute, $244 on Daytona on-demand and $265 on Modal.
